topicName: Layer 2 Attacks (ARP Spoofing, VLAN Hopping, STP Manipulation)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Layer 2 Attacks and Mitigations"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Layer 2 of the OSI model (Data Link Layer) relies heavily on trust. Protocols designed decades ago, such as ARP, DTP, and STP, often lack built-in authentication or integrity checks. This tutorial explores three critical Layer 2 attack vectors: ARP Spoofing, VLAN Hopping, and Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Manipulation, along with strategies to defend against them in enterprise networks."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Spoofing"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local area network. Because ARP is stateless, a host can process gratuitous ARP replies even if it never sent an ARP request. Attackers exploit this to associate their own MAC address with the IP address of a target, such as the default gateway."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Simulating ARP Spoofing with Scapy"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"from scapy.all import ARP, send
# Craft a forged ARP reply
# target_ip: IP of the victim (e.g., gateway)
# spoof_ip: IP to impersonate (e.g., target machine)
# mac: Attacker's MAC address
packet = ARP(op=2, pdst='192.168.1.1', hwdst='AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF', psrc='192.168.1.50')
send(packet, verbose=False)"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Impact: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, traffic interception, session hijacking, and Denial of Service (DoS)."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Defense: Implement Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches, which cross-references ARP packets with DHCP snooping bindings."},{"order":9,"type":"heading","text":"2. VLAN Hopping"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"VLAN hopping allows traffic from one VLAN to be seen by another without routing through a Layer 3 device. The two primary methods are Switch Spoofing (exploiting Dynamic Trunking Protocol) and Double Tagging (exploiting native VLAN behaviors)."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Switch Spoofing Attack Mechanics"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"If switch ports are configured with DTP in the 'desirable' or 'auto' mode by default, an attacker's machine can negotiate a trunk link with the switch. Once a trunk is established, the attacker can send and receive tagged frames across multiple VLANs."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Defense: Disable DTP explicitly on all user-facing access ports using the command 'switchport nonegotiate'."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Defense: Explicitly define access ports ('switchport mode access') and prune unused VLANs."},{"order":15,"type":"heading","text":"3. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Manipulation"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"STP prevents bridging loops in Layer 2 topologies by electing a Root Bridge and blocking redundant paths. In an STP manipulation attack, an attacker floods the network with superior Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs), forcing the network to recalculate the topology and making the attacker's system the Root Bridge."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"STP Attack Implications"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Traffic redirection through the attacker's machine for comprehensive MitM monitoring."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Topology destabilization leading to intermittent network outages."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Hardening STP Configurations"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"Switch(config)# spanning-tree portfast default
Switch(config)# spanning-tree bpduguard default"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Enabling PortFast ensures edge ports immediately transition to the forwarding state, and BPDU Guard shuts down any port that unexpectedly receives a BPDU, preventing unauthorized switches or attackers from manipulating the spanning tree."}]
